Chemiresistive gas sensors detect gases through the change in electrical resistance of a sensing material, most often a semiconducting metal oxide such as TiO2 or SnO2. Adsorbed or reacting molecules trap or donate conduction electrons near the surface, so the resistance shifts with gas exposure; supported metal or metal oxide particles are often added to improve sensitivity and selectivity. See also [Metal-support interactions](/papers/topics/metal-support-interactions/) and [Oxygen vacancies in oxides](/papers/topics/oxygen-vacancies-in-oxides/).

## Four-point probe study of TiO2(001) and Pd/TiO2(001) in UHV (2003)

McCormick, Kitchin, Barteau and Chen used a linear four-point probe together with Auger spectroscopy and STM in ultrahigh vacuum to study rutile TiO2(001) as a model oxygen sensor. Sputtering lowered both the surface O/Ti ratio (to about TiO1.5 after 2500 s) and the resistivity, while exposing a sputtered surface to 1.1 x 10<sup>-5</sup> Torr O2 at 300 K raised the resistivity irreversibly, with a transient that was better fit by dissociative (second-order) than molecular (first-order) adsorption kinetics. Pd particles annealed to 573 K (5 to 12 nm) enhanced the response to 2.5 x 10<sup>-7</sup> Torr O2, whereas as-deposited (1 to 6 nm) and 773 K annealed (10 to 23 nm) particles gave little enhancement, which the authors attribute to the number of Pd sites for O2 adsorption and spillover ([McCormick et al. 2003](/papers/mccormick2003/)). Summary: [mccormick2003](/papers/mccormick2003/).
